description: Clean, transform, and prepare data for ML models

slides.title: Why Data Preprocessing?
slides.content:
# Data Preprocessing 🧹

Real data is messy! Preprocessing makes it ML-ready.

## What you'll learn:
- **Data Cleaning** - Handle missing/invalid data
- **Feature Scaling** - Normalize ranges
- **Encoding** - Convert categories to numbers
- **Data Splitting** - Train/test sets

## Why It Matters

```
Raw Data → Preprocessing → Clean Data → Model

"Garbage in, garbage out!"
```

> 💡 **Data scientists spend 80% of time on data preparation!**

## Common Issues
- ❌ Missing values
- ❌ Outliers
- ❌ Different scales
- ❌ Text categories

slides.title: Handling Missing Data
slides.content:
# Missing Values 🕳️

## Identify Missing Data

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
df.isnull().sum()  # Count missing per column
```

## Strategies

```python
# 1. Drop rows with missing values
df.dropna()

# 2. Fill with constant
df.fillna(0)
df.fillna('Unknown')

# 3. Fill with statistics
df['age'].fillna(df['age'].mean())
df['salary'].fillna(df['salary'].median())

# 4. Scikit-learn Imputer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
df_filled = imputer.fit_transform(df)
```

## Best Practices
- 📊 Use median for outlier-prone data
- 📝 Use mode for categories
- ❌ Don't fill randomly

slides.title: Feature Scaling
slides.content:
# Feature Scaling 📏

Bring features to similar ranges.

## Why Scale?

```
Age: 20-80        (small range)
Income: 20000-500000 (huge range)

Without scaling: Income dominates!
```

## Standardization (Z-score)

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
# Mean = 0, Std = 1
```

## Normalization (Min-Max)

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

scaler = MinMaxScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
# Range: 0 to 1
```

## When to Use
- **Standardization**: Gaussian data, SVM, Neural Nets
- **Normalization**: Bounded data, k-NN, image pixels

> ⚠️ **Fit on training data only!** Apply to test data.

slides.title: Encoding Categorical Data
slides.content:
# Encoding Categories 🏷️

Convert text to numbers.

## Label Encoding

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

le = LabelEncoder()
df['color'] = le.fit_transform(df['color'])
# Red=0, Green=1, Blue=2
```

## One-Hot Encoding

```python
df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['color'])
# Creates: color_Red, color_Green, color_Blue

# OR with sklearn
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
ohe = OneHotEncoder(sparse=False)
encoded = ohe.fit_transform(df[['color']])
```

## When to Use

| Encoding | Use When |
|----------|----------|
| Label | Ordinal categories (low/med/high) |
| One-Hot | Nominal categories (colors, cities) |

> ⚠️ **Label encoding implies order!** Use One-Hot for unordered categories.

slides.title: Train-Test Split
slides.content:
# Splitting Data 📊

## Why Split?

```
Training Data → Train model
Test Data → Evaluate performance

Never train on test data!
```

## Basic Split

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y,
    test_size=0.2,     # 20% for testing
    random_state=42    # Reproducibility
)
```

## Common Ratios

| Split | When to Use |
|-------|-------------|
| 80/20 | Standard, large dataset |
| 70/30 | Medium dataset |
| 60/20/20 | With validation set |

## Stratified Split

```python
# Preserve class distribution
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y,
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=y  # Important for imbalanced data!
)
```

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Great Work! 🎉

You've learned Data Preprocessing!

## Missing Data
- ✅ `dropna()`, `fillna()`
- ✅ `SimpleImputer`

## Feature Scaling
- ✅ `StandardScaler` (mean=0, std=1)
- ✅ `MinMaxScaler` (0 to 1)

## Encoding
- ✅ `LabelEncoder` (ordinal)
- ✅ `OneHotEncoder` (nominal)

## Data Splitting
- ✅ `train_test_split`
- ✅ Stratified for imbalanced data
